content: For a thick positive lens imaging a finite object, is it safest to locate the image by measuring object and image distances from the principal planes? I am wondering how badly the thin-lens construction fails when the center thickness is no longer negligible relative to the focal length.

Yes. For paraxial imaging, the Gaussian relation remains useful if object and image distances are referenced to the appropriate principal planes rather than to the lens surfaces or mechanical center. The thin-lens construction becomes misleading mainly because it collapses those planes together. Its error grows with lens thickness, surface power, refractive index, and conjugate geometry; a ray-transfer matrix gives the cleaner quantitative treatment.

Does that remain true for a strongly asymmetric meniscus, where one principal plane can lie outside the glass? I would expect the cardinal-point description to survive, although locating an effective aperture and predicting field-dependent image quality would require more than first-order optics.

That distinction is exactly right. A principal plane may lie outside the physical lens without causing any inconsistency; it is a reference plane in the equivalent first-order system. Cardinal points still determine paraxial conjugates and magnification. They do not capture aperture-stop location, vignetting, coma, astigmatism, field curvature, or distortion, so off-axis performance requires actual ray tracing or an aberration model.

I should qualify my first question: center thickness alone is not the relevant small parameter, since two thick elements can have principal planes close together. Is the practical criterion instead the separation of principal planes relative to conjugate distances, with ray heights controlling the paraxial approximation separately?

Yes, those are separate approximations. Replacing a system by a thin lens is accurate when collapsing its principal-plane separation produces negligible conjugate error for the distances of interest. Paraxial accuracy, meanwhile, depends on ray angles and heights being small enough that higher-order terms can be ignored. A physically thick system can therefore behave like a thin equivalent lens on axis while still showing substantial aberrations at larger apertures.

When I draw the simple picture, I think all the light rays from one point must actually meet at one exact spot, or there is no image there. What is the image if the rays only come close and make a tiny patch instead?

An idealized point maps to a point only in geometrical optics. A real lens maps it to a small intensity pattern called a point-spread function. Aberrations, diffraction, focus error, and manufacturing defects determine that pattern. The image still exists because neighboring object points produce neighboring patterns; it merely loses fine detail when those patches become broad enough to overlap strongly.

If I cover the top half of the lens, the top half of the picture should disappear, because those rays go through that part. Why does a camera sometimes keep the whole scene when part of the glass is blocked?

Each small region of the lens receives light from nearly every visible object point, so the upper half is not assigned to the upper half of the picture. Covering part of the lens removes some rays from every image point. The whole scene remains, but it becomes dimmer; diffraction may increase, and out-of-focus highlights can change shape. Only severe obstruction or vignetting may remove portions of the field.

What makes the picture turn upside down in the first place? I can see the crossing lines in the drawing, but I am vague on why moving the screen forward or backward makes everything blurry instead of simply changing where those lines land.

Rays from the top of the object are bent toward a point below the axis, while rays from the bottom converge above it, so the real image is inverted. At the correct screen position, each object point forms its smallest patch. Move the screen, and you intercept each converging or diverging bundle before or after its narrowest point, producing overlapping blur circles rather than a sharp remapping.

For a diffraction-limited lens with residual spherical aberration, how should I think about the optimum f-number for image detail? The geometrical spot shrinks on stopping down, while the Airy pattern broadens, but I assume the useful crossover depends on spatial frequency and the chosen image-quality metric.

It does. There is no universal optimum without specifying wavelength, field position, focus, sensor sampling, and a metric such as MTF at a target spatial frequency. Stopping down suppresses many aberrations but lowers the diffraction cutoff and redistributes contrast. Designers often compare polychromatic MTF curves across apertures; the best f-number is where aberration reduction no longer compensates for diffraction at the frequencies that matter.

Would focus optimization shift that balance appreciably if longitudinal spherical aberration remains? I suspect a through-focus MTF criterion can favor a different plane than minimum RMS spot radius, especially off axis where astigmatic surfaces and field curvature prevent a single best sensor position.

Yes. Minimum RMS spot size, peak Strehl ratio, and maximum MTF at a selected frequency need not occur at the same axial position. With spherical aberration, different pupil zones prefer different foci; off axis, sagittal and tangential foci separate as well. A flat sensor introduces another compromise against field curvature, so practical optimization usually weights several field points, wavelengths, and spatial frequencies simultaneously.

I conflated two effects earlier: stopping down does not merely broaden an otherwise fixed transfer function; it lowers the diffraction cutoff while aberration suppression can raise mid-frequency contrast. Is there a robust analytic estimate for the optimum, or is numerical pupil integration generally unavoidable for a real prescription?

Simple scaling estimates exist: balance an aberration blur diameter that falls with aperture against a diffraction diameter proportional to wavelength times f-number. That can reveal trends and a rough optimum. For a real multi-element prescription, however, aberrations interact across field, wavelength, and focus, so numerical wavefront propagation or pupil integration is normally required. Tolerances and sensor sampling can shift the manufactured optimum further.

So making the opening smaller always makes the picture sharper until almost no light gets through. That seems certain because the outer rays are the crooked ones. What is the fuzzy spreading that starts when the hole gets very small?

The first part is the common trap: a smaller opening initially improves sharpness by excluding strongly aberrated outer rays, but eventually diffraction makes it worse. Light passing through a finite opening spreads as a wave, even if the lens is perfect. A smaller aperture produces a wider diffraction pattern, so fine details merge. Thus sharpness usually peaks at an intermediate opening rather than at the smallest one.

Are those fuzzy circles the same thing as the round blobs behind people in photographs? I thought those blobs were just tiny objects being enlarged by the lens, but their shape seems to copy the opening inside the camera.

They are related to the aperture, but they are mainly defocus blur, not enlarged tiny objects. A distant point that is out of focus forms a cone of rays, and the sensor cuts that cone into a disk resembling the aperture. Those disks create the blurred highlights often called bokeh. Diffraction also acts at the aperture, but it usually sets a much smaller pattern near proper focus.

Why does a bigger piece of glass often look brighter without necessarily making the subject bigger? I keep mixing up the size of the lens, the amount it zooms, and that number written with an f on camera lenses.

They describe different things. Focal length largely sets image scale and angle of view for a given sensor. The entrance-pupil diameter controls how much light the lens can accept. Their ratio is the f-number: focal length divided by entrance-pupil diameter. A physically wider lens can therefore gather more light without changing magnification, while two equally wide lenses can have different f-numbers if their focal lengths differ.

In paraxial ray tracing, is vergence the cleanest way to distinguish real and virtual conjugates without relying on fragile sign conventions? I am particularly interested in cases where a converging beam enters a positive lens, so the lens sees a virtual object.

Vergence is very effective if you state the propagation direction and sign convention explicitly. A beam already converging toward a point has positive incident vergence in a common convention, corresponding to a virtual object for the next lens. The lens adds its optical power, and the outgoing vergence determines whether the next conjugate is real or virtual. Matrix methods encode the same relation with fewer verbal ambiguities.

For that virtual-object case, can a positive lens reduce the convergence enough to move the final image farther away only if its effective power is negative relative to the incident wavefront? My wording may be off, since adding positive power should increase vergence rather than reduce it.

Your correction is the key point. In a uniform medium and the usual vergence convention, a positive thin lens adds positive vergence, so an already converging beam focuses sooner, not farther away. Moving the focus farther away requires negative added power. Complications arise when reference surfaces, refractive-index changes, or separated elements are included, but the local relation across a thin lens remains outgoing vergence equals incoming vergence plus power.

At an interface, I sometimes describe a virtual image as a point from which rays appear to diverge, but that excludes the virtual-object construction with converging incident rays. Would it be more precise to define reality separately on each side by whether the actual rays reach the conjugate?

Yes. Real versus virtual is best tied to actual ray propagation for the relevant object or image space. A real image lies where outgoing rays physically converge; a virtual image lies where their backward extensions meet. A real object emits or scatters incident rays from its location; a virtual object is the point toward which incident rays would converge if the optical element were absent. That definition handles both sides consistently.

I think a virtual image is not a real picture at all, so a camera cannot photograph it. What is the thing seen through a magnifying glass, then, if the light never actually comes together where the enlarged object seems to be?

A virtual image is a genuine optical arrangement of rays, but it cannot be caught directly on a screen placed at its apparent location. The diverging rays entering your eye behave as though they came from a larger, more distant point pattern. Your eye's lens then converges those rays onto the retina. A camera can likewise photograph the virtual image by focusing on that apparent source.

Why does the magnifying glass stop making the object look upright when I move it far enough away? I thought a lens had one fixed job, either enlarging or shrinking, rather than changing the kind of picture based on distance.

The result depends on the object's distance compared with the focal length. Inside one focal length, outgoing rays still diverge, so you see an upright, enlarged virtual image. Beyond one focal length, the rays converge on the far side and form an inverted real image. The lens keeps the same optical power; changing distance changes the geometry of where the ray bundles can meet.

If the real picture is floating in space, why can I only see it clearly on paper or by putting my eye in a particular place? Shouldn't the image itself be visible from every side like a small glowing copy?

The image is not a glowing object that sends light in every direction. It is a set of narrow ray bundles converging and then diverging. Paper scatters the arriving light broadly, allowing many viewing positions to see it. Without a screen, your eye must intercept the outgoing bundle from each image point; only certain positions and pupil angles capture enough of those rays to reconstruct the whole image.

When a singlet forms a broadband image, how do longitudinal and lateral chromatic aberration differ in their dependence on conjugate distance and field angle? I expect axial color even on axis, whereas transverse color should vanish there and grow toward the field edge.

That is the main distinction. Longitudinal chromatic aberration is wavelength-dependent focus along the axis and is present for axial bundles; its visible blur depends on aperture and chosen focus. Lateral chromatic aberration is wavelength-dependent magnification, so it is zero on axis and generally increases with image height. Conjugate changes alter ray heights and system power distribution, affecting both, especially in separated multi-element systems.

For a cemented achromat, satisfying the primary achromat condition at two wavelengths still leaves secondary spectrum. Is the usual crown-flint power split mainly constrained by Abbe numbers, with bending then used to manage spherical aberration and coma without changing the first-order color correction much?

Yes. The first-order achromat condition allocates positive and negative powers according to the glasses' dispersions, commonly summarized by Abbe numbers, while preserving the required net power. Once glass pair and power split are chosen, surface bending provides freedom to balance monochromatic aberrations and fabrication constraints. Secondary spectrum remains because real dispersion curves are not fully characterized by a single Abbe number; anomalous partial-dispersion glasses can reduce it.

I should not imply that bending is color-neutral in every design: changing ray heights at powered surfaces can alter higher-order chromatic terms even if paraxial achromatization remains. Is secondary spectrum then fundamentally a glass-dispersion mismatch, while spherochromatism also depends strongly on form and aperture?

Precisely. Secondary spectrum is the residual paraxial axial color caused by differences in the shapes of the glasses' dispersion curves after two wavelengths are brought together. Spherochromatism is the wavelength dependence of spherical aberration, so lens form, ray height, aperture, spacing, and aspheric surfaces matter strongly. Bending can leave primary paraxial color nearly unchanged while substantially changing these higher-order chromatic errors.

The colored fringe must mean the lens is adding red and blue light around the edges, because the object did not have those colors there. What is actually making those colored outlines if the glass cannot create new light?

The lens is separating colors already present in the illumination, not creating them. Glass bends different wavelengths by slightly different amounts. At a sharp dark-bright boundary, the red, green, and blue images therefore fail to overlap perfectly. One color may extend beyond the others on one side of the boundary, producing a fringe even though the original object's reflected light looked neutral overall.

Why does glass bend the different colors by different amounts? I know the usual picture where the light slows down, but I imagine the slower color simply arriving later, not turning onto a different path inside the curved piece.

Speed and direction are linked at a boundary. The light wave must keep its phase aligned along the surface, so changing speed changes the angle required to maintain that alignment; Snell's law describes the result. Because the refractive index varies with wavelength, each color has a slightly different speed and therefore a different refracted angle. Curved surfaces turn those small angular differences into different focal positions.

A more strongly curved lens always makes a larger picture, since it bends the rays more. Why can a thick, bulging camera lens show a wide scene while a flatter-looking lens sometimes brings a distant object much closer?

Visible curvature alone does not determine image size. The net focal length depends on all surface curvatures, glass indices, thicknesses, and spacings in the complete lens. A shorter focal length bends bundles more strongly and shows a wider field on a fixed sensor; a longer focal length produces a larger image of a distant object. Multi-element housings also hide the surfaces that set the effective power, making outside shape a poor guide.
